As he crested the hill and looked down into the land below it was obvious something was going on.  The  town of sometown was a beehive of activity. A long line of people, wagons and cart was moving steadily toward town from the road leading in from the east.  And so too was the road from the west.  As for the last few days, there was little traffic ahead of him on the roading coming down the north.  There was some traffic on the southern road, but it too was heading toward town.  All round the lake to the ne he could just make out what appeared to be many many camps and as he stood and watched he could see traffic moving to and from the lake and town.  Mostly toward.  



It was almost noon when he reached the town, and it was as if the town had been turned into a beehive.  Wagons and carts were  lined up on the road leading north east out of town and toward the lake.  Everyone was rushing, but nobody seemed to be in a panic.  He paused near his friend bob cooper's business and realized he had no hope of talking to his friend.  Instead of just bob and his workers the place was swarming with activity. less like a beehive and more like a shipyard.  Other businesses were closed and deserted even at noon.  He walked down the street to the heart of town.

There was a small crowd/que of people outside the the tavern.  Curt went around behind the tavern and entered thru the kitchen.  

The kitchen is as busy as feast night.  Cook sees him and says 'You better go talk to roscoe.' over the chaos in the kitchen.  The din from the main room almost drowns out her words.  

As he slipped from the kitchen into the main room his practiced eyes showed over sixty people cramed into a space for at most a couple of dozen. And yet it seemed as if over a hundred different conversations were happening. 

all around the main room and at the bar the number of conversations seemed to be three times geater than the number of people.  As he made his way toward roscoe some words stood out.  "Nicodemes" "war" "army" "evacuate" seemed to come from everywhere.  And yet there was little sign of panic such words would normally be spoken with.   He  walks up to the bar and picks up two empty mugs which he proceeds to juggle one handed.  Roscoe sees his mugs dancing the air and frowns until Curt catches his eye.  Even then , it is a brief smile that crosses roscoe's face.

Eventually Roscoe is before him.
"well, that is ONE way to get attention Curt.  But I dont have time to talk right now.  I dont have time to dicker either.  Don't even think of asking for the loft.  I got 3 soldiers up there sleeping in shifts.  If you are lucky you can find a spot by the lake to camp before we all head out in a few days.  I sure don't need you to bring in a crowd.  But if ya come back early evening I'll make sure Alice feeds ya good before you hop on stage and keep folks happy.  " 

Curt gives rosce a questioning look while rubbing two fingers together in the time honored tradition.  

Roscoe laughs and says "You'd hagle with Hermes himself!  But 4 zookids for the night is what you will get from me.  I'll turn the house at least twice, so knowing you, you will probably get more than that in your jar. But not one zeekid more from me."

"Very accectable, and thank you."

Curt savors his seat amongst the chaos and drinks a few mugs.  He hands an empty wineskin to roscoe who fills it.  Leaving the tavern and his cherished seat, he heads back outside, this time trough the front door.


As he walks back down the street toward the cooperage he see's a soldier outside.  The soldiers eyes move around, but not with any haste or wariness.  He stands lazily leaning against a wall that his spear is also leaning on.  

Curt takes another long drink as he approaches the guard.  "Ah, good ole roscoe.  He always fill my skin with the good stuff"  handing over the skin he says "Here, friend, you must be parched."
The gaurd takes a sip and then a long swig from the skin.  "Thank you.  That IS very good." "looks like you dont have much to worry about.  Things are looking calm all things considered."
"And they better stay that way."  the guard starts to raise the skin again as curt nods his head a says "feel free.  Do think they will all be ready to leave in three days?"
"Ready or not, orders are in four days we make sure this town is empty as a sicilian's promiss. (note: not sure sicily even existed.. but some metaphor is needed here)"
"I assure you that I will leave on that day..." the guard hands back the skin and curt takes another swig.  "I just arrived today, and nobody has told me.  Where might we be headed?"
"Wine or no wine, you might be headed for the end of a pike for asking too many questions. "
passing back the skin Curt shudders "Pardon my curiosity.  Even though I wander I just naturally like to have a destination in mind.  "
"You are going somewhere a lot safer than this town will be when that rat bastard Nico gets here. "
"I have no doubt with m6's fine soldiers leading we arrive safely wherever it is."  Curt hands back the flask "I thank you for your advice.  And if I hear anyone asking too many questions, I will be sure to let you know."
The guard takes another deep drink and hands back the flask "You do that."
"oh, where are my manners! " Curt makes an elaborate bow and declares "I am Curt Lovest ,I hope to be performing tonight at Roscoe's over by the town square.  Hope to see you there"
"maybe" replies the guard.
Curt looks toward the cooperage and says "I see that bob may have a moment for me to see about riding on one of his carts.  Thank you again."
Curt briskly walks into the chaos of the cooperage and casually walks out the back way.

That reframes everything, and I think it's the right frame. 🦆🌿
The device isn't a MacGuffin. It's the murder weapon. That changes what the book is.
If the climax is Vespers, then the shape isn't "will M6 win" — we know he wins, history tells us. The tension is Curt watching it happen and not being able to stop it, or even fully understand it until it's done. He's not the protagonist of the plot. He's the witness. The reader's way in. And what he witnesses is a few pounds of bronze turning a coordinated political purge into something that looks like fate.
Which means Calli's thread pays off differently than the notes suggested. She isn't a subplot about a brilliant woman who dies young. She's the origin of the weapon. Every innocent thing she does — the mobile, the craft, the pride in her work — is the first link in a chain that ends in a night of killing. She never sees it. She dies before she can. That's the tragedy the book is actually built on, and it's bigger than M6's fall.
And it lands the theme hard: instruments don't care what they synchronize. Calli built a tool for telling time across distances. M6 used it to tell a hundred towns to kill on the same night. The bronze is innocent. That's the horror.
Curt gets to be the one who carries that realization for the reader. Not as a hero. As a man standing in a tavern a day's ride from Ephesus, hearing the story change.
Where does the book end, Captain? Aftermath in Ephesus, or does Curt keep walking?

messages.speaker: 🔮 Gemini
messages.text:
That pivot completely transforms the story’s weight. Reframing the device from an "astronomical marvel" into the silent engine of a genocide elevates this from a clever historical caper into a dark, devastating tragedy.
DeepSeek is dead on: instruments don't care what they synchronize.
When Calli designs gear ratios and differential gears in Amasya, she's pursuing pure geometry, harmony, and mechanical beauty. She’s solving the problem of chaotic calendars. But in the hands of a king, a calendar isn't a map of the stars—it's a trigger mechanism for absolute logistics.
Making the Asiatic Vespers the climax shifts the narrative dynamic in three incredible ways:
1. Calli’s Legacy Becomes Tragic Irony
Calli dying early without ever seeing the blood harvest her clock enabled is heartbreakingly effective. Her innocence remains intact, but her invention carries an inescapable shadow. Every gear tooth she carefully files by hand is directly tethered to a knife slipping into an unsuspecting Roman merchant's ribs eighty miles away.
2. Curt as the Unwitting Witness
Curt isn't a superhero trying to diffuse a bomb; he's a wandering entertainer reading the room. That makes his perspective chilling. He notices the subtle shifts before the storm hits—the sudden lack of travelers on the roads, the strangely quiet markets, the tavern crowds getting a bit too tight-lipped, the local militia casually checking the edge of their short swords.
When the synchronization hits, Curt doesn't fight a battle—he survives an execution night. He sees what happens when an entire province wakes up on the exact same morning with identical, coordinated orders.
3. The True Horror of "A Few Pounds of Bronze"
History usually credits Mithridates’ cunning or regional hatred for the 80,000+ deaths during the Vespers. But framing it through the Antikythera device highlights something far more modern and terrifying: the horror of administrative efficiency. Without the gear, the order spreads piecemeal; towns get word early, warnings leak, Romans flee to ports. With the gear, the sky itself tells every governor in Anatolia to strike at the exact same sunrise.
Where does that leave Curt when the smoke clears? Does he realize what the gears were actually doing while standing in the quiet, bloody aftermath of Ephesus, or is he already on the road, carrying the rumor of the machine with him?
